title: Course Catalog & Student Resources — Start with Your Goal
body:
New to AI? Start AI Basics at lesson 01. No experience or paid AI plan is needed to begin.

Choose See more to open the full catalog below. Pick one useful task; you do not need to finish every course.

Choose something useful to work on. Our programming is always free; you do not need to complete the whole catalog. Most lessons work with any suitable AI assistant.

Two student plugins: help when you want it

  • Guide Me — your coach, research assistant and thought partner. Bring a question, a lesson, a draft or a problem; ask for explanations and help thinking it through.
  • Your Learning Path — share your goals, experience and interests to build a personalized lesson plan. Save the plan and bring its handoff to Guide Me if useful.

Open Your Big Lever AI Guides — downloads and installation. Download either Version 1 ZIP from that lesson’s Resources and follow its installation directions. These optional plugins currently install in your own ChatGPT account; available features and account limits apply. You can use the rest of our lessons without them, with another suitable assistant. Installed copies do not automatically update. We cannot see your private chats.

For educators and community leaders

Adapt our free AI lessons for your own learners. Explore complete lesson materials, worked examples, and our approach to reviewing and improving them—with clear notes on what we’ve tested.

Explore BLI for Educators. Reuse and adapt our original educational material with attribution under CC BY 4.0. The repository explains the permissions; no community membership is needed to read it.

I am new to AI

  • Understand what AI can help with — useful capabilities and limits
  • Choose an assistant and begin — no paid plan is required to start
  • Try a first useful task — use supplied facts, revise and check
  • Build a clearer prompt — purpose, context and useful output
  • Use a guided conversation — ask questions, explore options and optionally build a prompt together
  • Work from notes or files — check what the assistant can read
  • Give useful instructions — separate preferences from facts
  • Organize continuing work — saved Projects or a pasted-context alternative
  • Check and keep your result — facts, fit and actual actions

Everyday work and career

  • Write emails you can reuse — keep your voice and changing facts separate
  • Tailor your résumé — match real experience to a role
  • Practice an interview — answer in your own words and retry
  • Improve your LinkedIn profile — make truthful experience clear
  • Create a presentation from notes — build an audience-focused argument

Research, learning and decisions

  • Build a Project Brain — organize sources and approved learning around a topic
  • Research a topic or industry — bound the question and check sources
  • Prepare a briefing — help a reader make a decision
  • Compare options — requirements, preferences and uncertainty
  • Practice a negotiation — rehearse with goals and boundaries
  • Explore contrasting viewpoints — simulated lenses, not independent experts
  • Keep your decision reasoning — record reasons and conditions for revisiting

Business ideas and customer learning

  • Clarify a venture problem — separate observations from assumptions
  • Prepare customer questions — learn about real recent behavior
  • Organize customer observations — separate facts, interpretations and gaps
  • Understand customer differences — group behavior without inventing evidence
  • Examine alternatives — competitors, workarounds and doing nothing
  • Plan a landing page — offer, proof and next action
  • Draft and test ad messages — supported claims and meaningful variants

Organizing work and building products

  • Choose what to build first — needs, dependencies and bounded priorities
  • Understand stakeholder needs — outcomes and failure checks
  • Examine financial data — classify transactions and reconcile totals
  • Reuse a method that worked — test it on changed inputs

Building with code

  • Build a useful small tool — define behavior and test actual execution
  • Understand an unfamiliar codebase — trace explanations to actual code
  • Save your first code version — inspect intended files and record a commit
  • Prepare a change for review — inspect the actual hosted change

Coding setup: repository work needs Git and a terminal or editor; hosted review also needs a code-host account and permission to contribute. A personal tool needs a suitable way to run it. Each lesson explains its requirements; ask for setup help before running commands. Coding is optional elsewhere.

Prefer a connected learning path?

The seven mini-courses guide you through exercises stored once in the Exercise Library. Follow a path or open one exercise directly. MC labels are mini-course identifiers; numbers do not impose a sequence.

  • Everyday AI — Practical Examples — Apply the basics to a personally useful email or résumé, then check and improve it.
  • Startup Foundations — Develop a customer-grounded problem hypothesis and a useful next investigation.
  • Digital Marketing — Turn a supported offer into an honest message and an informative test.
  • AI Tools and Workflows — Produce a source-grounded synthesis that helps a particular audience make sense of a topic.
  • Coding for Shippers — Make a small reversible software change and prepare it for review.
  • Prompting and Workflows — Preserve a method that proved useful, then adapt it without losing its limits.
  • Product Thinking — Connect stakeholder evidence to a bounded scope and a defensible first priority.

Quick reference

Plain-language glossary — look up unfamiliar words when needed.

Coming Soon

New Venture Planning, Prod-ject Managing and Vibe Coding for Shippers are future full-length courses. Their landing pages are available, but the full lessons are not. No launch date is announced. The practical exercises and mini-courses above are available now.

Help improve the alpha

Tell us what helped, what was unclear or what you would like to learn next. Comment here, or choose Email lesson feedback at the end of any classroom lesson. Include the lesson link and a brief description. Please leave out private material.
